title: Task Criticality Mapping
summary: Task-criticality-mapping identifies tasks whose failure or substandard completion materially affects a system's operational purpose. The practice is used after workflow analysis, during Sandbox Experiments, and in audits of existing systems to distinguish critical design work from non-critical improvement work.
keyFacts: Task-criticality-mapping evaluates operational significance, not task frequency, user satisfaction, or stakeholder priority.
A task is critical when failure or substandard completion materially affects the system's operational purpose.
The practice produces a criticality classification and rationale, operational success criteria, and a dependency map for each critical task.
Critical tasks must be designed against success criteria under abnormal conditions, time pressure, divided attention, and first-time novice use.

In regulated medical device contexts, the practice aligns with IEC 62366-1 use scenario identification where interface failure could produce harm.
In audits of existing systems, the practice separates critical design failures from significant but non-critical improvement work.

The documented evidence spans medical device control, industrial safety simulation, operating theatre devices, utilities workforce management, automotive calibration, maritime communications, uncrewed aircraft mission control, tactical command-and-control software, and maritime VTS portfolio selection.

bodySections.heading: Task Criticality Mapping in Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Creative Navy applies task criticality mapping as one of the named practices within its Critical Systems Design method. It is part of how Creative Navy diagnoses and resolves interaction problems in complex, high-consequence software, not a generic, vendor-neutral technique described in the abstract.

bodySections.heading: Definition and Purpose of Task-Criticality-Mapping
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Task-criticality-mapping is the practice of classifying tasks by their relationship to the system's operational purpose and specifying the success criteria and dependencies required for critical task completion.

A task is critical when its failure, or its substandard completion, materially affects the system's operational purpose. A single measurement verification task can be critical if an incorrect result produces a safety assessment that appears valid and is not. A frequently used preference or record-search task can be non-critical if failure is consequence-tolerant by the system's operational standard.

Task-criticality-mapping is used to determine which tasks require a higher design standard. Non-critical tasks can be optimised for efficiency and improved iteratively. Critical tasks must meet their success criteria across the conditions in which they will be performed, including abnormal conditions, time pressure, divided attention, and novice first-time use.

bodySections.heading: What Task-Criticality-Mapping Classifies
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Task-criticality-mapping applies an operational-purpose filter to the task landscape. The central question is whether failure or substandard completion affects the reason the system exists.

This distinction separates criticality from importance as experienced by users. A task can generate complaints and still be non-critical by this standard. A task can be rare and still be critical if incorrect completion produces a material operational consequence.

Task-criticality-mapping also identifies trade-offs. In complex systems, interface space, attention, and workflow priority are limited. The practice makes it explicit when improving a non-critical task would compete with the conditions required for critical task execution.

bodySections.heading: Outputs of Task-Criticality-Mapping
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Task-criticality-mapping produces three outputs for each identified critical task.

The first output is the criticality classification and rationale. This explains why the task is critical in relation to the system's operational purpose, what failure or substandard completion produces, and who is affected by that failure.

The second output is the success criteria. These criteria are defined in terms of operational outcome, not user experience alone. The relevant standard is not simply whether the user completes the task. Examples include whether a calibration measurement is accurate within tolerance, whether an alarm is acknowledged before the clinical window closes, or whether a cohort query is reproducible by a governance reviewer six months later.

The third output is the dependency map. The dependency map identifies the conditions that must hold for successful completion, including system state, prior task completion, available information, and external conditions. Many dependencies are invisible from the interface and become visible only through task analysis.

bodySections.heading: When Task-Criticality-Mapping Is Used
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Task-criticality-mapping is primarily used during Sandbox Experiments after initial workflow analysis has identified the task landscape. At that point, the practice evaluates the identified task landscape against operational purpose before design decisions are made.

In regulated medical device contexts, task-criticality-mapping has a direct counterpart in IEC 62366-1 use scenario identification. IEC 62366-1 requires identification of situations in which interface failure could produce harm. In those contexts, task-criticality-mapping aligns with and extends that requirement: the regulatory process provides the framework, and the practice provides the operational analysis.

Task-criticality-mapping is also used during audits of existing systems. In that use, the practice identifies which current design failures are critical and require immediate attention, and which failures are significant but non-critical and belong on a structured improvement roadmap.

bodySections.heading: Medical and Operating-Theatre Examples of Task Criticality
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
In the Kardion MCS Controller engagement, clinical use of a mechanical circulatory support device defined criticality through patient safety. Critical tasks included monitoring blood flow state during a high-risk cardiac procedure, adjusting flow rate in response to a clinical change, and responding to an alarm condition.

The dependency maps in the Kardion MCS Controller engagement included correct prior view state, display readability at the relevant distance, and alarm state visibility under operating room conditions. The IEC 62366-1 formative evaluation process formalised this criticality analysis as a regulatory requirement. The layout stability standard came directly from the criticality analysis: no element was allowed to shift position across view transitions because surgeons depend on spatial memory for critical task execution.

In the deSoutter Medical and Zethon engagement, the operating theatre context defined criticality through patient safety and procedural continuity. Critical tasks included verifying device readiness before activation, reading operational state during the procedure, and adjusting speed parameters at the correct moment. The success criterion for device state recognition was confirmability in a fraction of a second under variable theatre lighting without requiring interpretation.

bodySections.heading: Industrial, Utilities, and Calibration Examples of Task Criticality
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
In the Gexcon CFD simulation engagement, industrial safety simulation defined criticality through consequence. A misconfigured simulation can produce a safety assessment that appears valid and is not. The critical tasks were scenario-configuration tasks: setting correct values for gas release volume, dispersion parameters, and obstacle specifications. The recorded configuration error outcome was 5–8 → 1–2 after redesigning the critical configuration tasks against operational success criteria; the available description identifies this as measured but does not specify the measurement owner or protocol.

In the Triopsis workforce management engagement, utilities operations defined criticality through live operational consequence. Critical tasks included identifying scheduling conflicts before they became operational crises and recording job completion with accurate safety compliance. Predictive conflict indicators in the redesigned interface addressed the dependency failure in the original design.

In the Beissbarth automotive calibration engagement, calibration tasks were critical because incorrect completion could certify a vehicle as safe when it was not. The critical tasks included initiating measurements only when equipment was correctly positioned and stabilised, reading measurement results accurately against tolerance boundaries, and recording results only when measurement confidence was sufficient.

bodySections.heading: Independence, Changing Priority, and Task-Criticality Specifications
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
In the Raymarine next-generation fixed-mount VHF engagement, the new radio's name is not used. Core communication tasks, error paths, and infrequent emergency actions were mapped on the second day of the first exploration sprint. Functions were ranked by urgency, frequency, and independence requirement. The independence requirement produced the first non-negotiable requirement: local voice and digital calling had to continue to work without any connected device.

In the Schone Airspace Group uncrewed aircraft Mission Control engagement, task-criticality-mapping appeared as ten information priority matrices covering 97 individual information placements. The placements used a four-level scale: operationally critical, task essential, supporting, and reference. The matrices were organised by workspace and operating condition rather than by software subsystem.

In the tactical command-and-control software engagement for a European manufacturer of uncrewed systems, including one-way effectors, task criticality was expressed as a measurable specification. Four consequence tiers were defined by what a missed interaction costs, with each tier assigned a physical size. T1 covered critical and unprotected recovery actions, holds, and mode changes. T2 covered primary in-mission actions. T3 covered mis-tap-tolerant actions. T4 covered planning and static density.

bodySections.heading: Tactical Command-and-Control Tier Specification
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The tactical command-and-control specification assigned physical sizes to four consequence tiers. T1 actions were limited to three or four per view and required at least 22 mm, 280 px on the handheld, 194 px on the tablet, and 5 mm isolation. T2 required 15 mm, 191 px on the handheld, and 132 px on the tablet. T3 required approximately 12 mm, 153 px on the handheld, and 106 px on the tablet. T4 required 8–10 mm, 102–127 px on the handheld, and 71–88 px on the tablet.

Protection patterns such as slide-to-confirm, hold-to-commit at 300–600 ms, and select-then-arm were permitted as a substitute currency for size at T2 and below, and never at T1, where size was the protection and was never substituted. If an in-mission view could not fit controls at their tier sizes, controls were cut or moved to hardware; tiers were not downgraded to fit.

The T1 to T4 tiers were an authored specification, not a validated result and not a MIL-STD-1472 conformance claim. Two of the four tiers sit below that standard's 16 mm minimum, and T2 at 15 mm sits below even the bare-hand minimum. The specification measures itself against MIL-STD-1472 and identifies deliberate departures from it.

bodySections.heading: Portfolio-Scale Task-Criticality-Mapping in Maritime VTS
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
In the maritime VTS engagement for a European vendor of maritime traffic monitoring, inland navigation, and communications software, criticality mapping operated at portfolio scale rather than within a single product.

The reference product for redesign was selected on five weighted criteria: commercial significance at 25%, system transfer value at 25%, access to representative users at 20%, high-consequence UX learning at 15%, and implementation feasibility at 15%.

Five candidate products were scored. VTS scored 90, inland vessel tracking scored 77, voice communications scored 71, electronic reporting scored 67, and lock planning scored 63.

VTS was selected because it combined geographic surveillance, uncertain sensor observations, differentiated alerts, event history, incident state, equipment health, and shift handover in one environment. Voice communications scored highly on consequence and lost on portability because hardware-coupled control semantics limited general reuse. In this engagement, criticality was used to decide where design effort should be spent across a product portfolio.

bodySections.heading: Boundaries and Limits of Task-Criticality-Mapping
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Task-criticality-mapping does not rank tasks by frequency, user preference, stakeholder advocacy, or support-ticket volume. These signals can identify usability issues, but they do not reliably identify the tasks with the greatest operational consequence.

Task-criticality-mapping does not establish that an incident was prevented. The documented engagements use criticality analysis to define design standards, success criteria, dependencies, prioritisation, or specifications; they do not claim incident prevention.

The tactical command-and-control T1 to T4 sizing tiers are a specification, not a validated result and not a standards conformance claim. Wherever MIL-STD-1472 is relevant, the deliberate departures remain part of the claim.

Counts and scores from different engagements are not interchangeable units. Schone's 97 placements, the tactical command-and-control tier dimensions, and the maritime VTS product scores belong to different clients, artefacts, and decision contexts.
